content: The risk of maternal mortality and morbidity is higher following a caesarean section compared to vaginal delivery. With the increasing frequency of caesarean sections, it is critical to minimize risks to the mother. This review focuses on various methods of skin preparation to prevent infections after caesarean sections. It is an update of a previous review published in 2018. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of different antiseptic agents, methods of application, and forms of antiseptics used for preoperative skin preparation in preventing post-caesarean infections. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that evaluated any type of preoperative skin preparation, including comparisons between different antiseptic agents (e.g., alcohol, povidone-iodine), application methods (e.g., scrubbing, painting, or draping), and forms of antiseptics (e.g., liquid, powder). Studies involving the preparation of the incision area were included, but those focusing on preoperative handwashing by the surgical team or preoperative bathing were excluded. The review included 13 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 6938 women undergoing caesarean sections. Data from 12 trials (6916 women) were analyzed. These trials were conducted between 1983 and 2016 in various countries, including the USA, India, Egypt, Nigeria, South Africa, France, Denmark, and Indonesia. Most studies had a low risk of bias, although some concerns were raised regarding detection bias. The length of hospital stay was reported in only one comparison. Antiseptic Agents: 1. Parachlorometaxylenol with iodine versus iodine alone: The evidence was of very low certainty, making it unclear whether parachlorometaxylenol combined with iodine reduced the incidence of surgical site infections (risk ratio [RR] 0.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.04 to 2.99; 1 trial, 50 women) or endometritis (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.38; 1 trial, 50 women) compared to iodine alone. Adverse events (maternal or neonatal) were not reported. 2. Chlorhexidine gluconate versus povidone-iodine: Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that chlorhexidine gluconate probably slightly reduces the incidence of surgical site infections compared to povidone-iodine (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.91; 8 trials, 4323 women). Sensitivity analysis, excluding trials with a high risk of bias, still showed a potential reduction in surgical site infections (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.23; 4 trials, 2037 women). Low-certainty evidence indicated that chlorhexidine gluconate may make little or no difference in the incidence of endometritis (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.86; 3 trials, 2484 women). It is uncertain whether chlorhexidine gluconate reduces maternal skin irritation or allergic reactions (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.46; 3 trials, 1926 women; very low-certainty evidence). One small study (60 women) reported reduced bacterial growth 18 hours after caesarean section in women who had chlorhexidine gluconate preparation compared to povidone-iodine preparation (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.70). Methods: 1. Drape versus no drape: Low-certainty evidence suggested that using a drape before surgery, compared to no drape, may make little or no difference in the incidence of surgical site infections (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.71; 3 trials, 1373 women). Moderate-certainty evidence indicated that the use of a drape probably makes little or no difference to the length of hospital stay (mean difference [MD] 0.10 days, 95% CI -0.27 to 0.46; 1 trial, 603 women). One trial compared an alcohol scrub and iodophor drape with a five-minute iodophor scrub alone and reported no surgical site infections in either group (79 women; very low-certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether a combination of a one-minute alcohol scrub and a drape reduces the incidence of metritis compared to a five-minute scrub alone (RR 1.62, 95% CI 0.29 to 9.16; 1 trial, 79 women). Adverse events (maternal or neonatal) were not reported. Authors' Conclusions: Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that chlorhexidine gluconate is probably slightly more effective than povidone-iodine in reducing the incidence of surgical site infections when used for preoperative skin preparation before caesarean sections. However, for other outcomes, there was insufficient evidence from the included RCTs. Most of the evidence was of very low or low certainty, limiting confidence in the findings and highlighting the need for further high-quality research. Future research should prioritize well-designed RCTs with larger sample sizes to address key questions, such as comparing different types of antiseptics (e.g., iodine versus chlorhexidine) and application methods (e.g., scrubbing, swabbing, or draping). Two ongoing studies were identified, and their results will be incorporated into future updates of this review.
